Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA corner Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City http: /mwu.dilg.com.ph DILG OPINION No. 70 s. 2023 HON. AMENAH F. PANGANDAMAN Secretary Department of Budget and Management Boncodin Hall, General Solano Street San Miguel, Manila Dear Sec. Pangandaman: This has reference to the letter dated June 5, 2023 from Vice Mayor Rosalita T. Nunez of General Santos City requesting for clarification on the following, quoted hereunder in toto: 1. Who hires the JO and COS in the Office of the Vice Mayor and the Sanggunian, when the source of funds is from the Legislative allocations? 2. Are Local Governments included in JMC No. 2, S. 2020 of COA and DBM, the Updated Rules and Regulations Governing Contracts of Service (COS) and Job Orders (JO) workers in the Government, as amended by JMC No. 2, s.2022, November IO, 2022, considering that there is no employer-employee relationship in JO and COS, making Section 77 of LGC 1991 qualified? 3. In the case of a supplemental budget, when the allocation already had a prior approval, in this case funds for the salaries and wages for JO and COS, can it still be changed without violating the law? And 4. Will the hired JO and COS under contract by the Local Chief Executive needs the imprimatur of the Sanggunian, even when the same as the Vice Mayor's, the funds for the salaries and wages of the same have been approved already in the executive budget and what is in countenance is an allocation under a supplemental budget? The herein matter stemmed from the seemingly conflicting views between the view of the Department and the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) on who has the power between the Mayor and Vice Mayor to hire COS and JOS. It must be recalled that the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) in its letter dated February 17, 2023, signed by Director Ria V. Bansigan of DBM Region-I, to Vice Mayor Simplicio L. Rosario of Binmaley, Pangasinan. with DMS Reference No.: 2023- ROI-0017822-E, citing the case of Atienza vs. Villarosa', has opined that: G.R. NO. 161081, May IO, 2005 "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.. 8876-34-54

Corollary, the Supreme Court ruled in the case of Atienza vs. Villarosa that "while the Governor has the authority to appoint officials and employees whose salaries are paid out of the provincial funds, this does not extend to the officials and employees of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan because such authority is lodged with the Vice-Governor. In the same manner, the authority to appoint casual and job order employees of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan belongs to the Vice-Governor." Said SC ruling is cited in the Frequently Asked Questions section of the BOM for LGUs, 2016 Edition, as circularized under Local Budget Circular No. 112 dated June IO, 2016, to wit: "The authority to appoint casual and job order employees of the Local Sanggunian belongs to the Vice-MayorNice-Governor. The authority of the Vice-GovernorNice-Mayor to appoint officials and employees of the local Sanggunian is anchored on the fact that the salaries of these employees are derived from the appropriation specifically for the said local legislative body. It is the source of their salaries which sets the employees and officials of the local Sanggunian apart from the other employees and officials of the LGU. Accordingly, the appointing power of the Vice-MayorNice-Governor is limited to those employees of the local Sanggunian, as well as those of the Office of the Vice-MayorNice-Governor, whose salaries are paid out of the funds appropriated for the Sanggunian Bayan/Panlungsod/PanIaIawigan. As a corollary, if the salary of an employee or official is charged against the municipal/city/provincial funds, even if this employee reports to the Vice- mayorNice-Governor or is assigned to his office, the Mayor/Governor retains the authority to appoint the said employee pursuant to Sections 455(b)(v); and 465)(b)(v) of the LGC." The said letter is in response to the query of Mayor Rosario on whether or not the Municipal Vice-Mayor has the authority to hire job order workers (not casual employees) assigned at the legislative offices and whose salaries are sourced from the appropriation of the Offices of the Vice-Mayor, Sangguniang Bayan and the Secretary to the Sangguniang Bayan, where Mayor Rosario cited this Department's Legal Opinion No. 89, series of 2022 — opining that it is the Mayor who has the authority to hire casual employees in the sanggunian and Office of the Vice-Mayor that are not provided plantilla and hired through job order contracts regardless of the source of funds. We confirm that the determining factor on who will appoint an employee is the source of fund as held by the SC in the case of Atienza vs. Villarosa. In fact, we categorized the employees of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan and the Office of the Vice Governor as follows: a. Employees of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan and of the Office of the Vice GovernorNice Mayor whose salaries are paid out of the provincial funds; Page 2 of 7

b. Employees of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan and of the Office of the Vice Governor whose salaries are paid out of the funds appropriated for the Sangguniang Panlalawigan; c. Casual Employees in the Sangguniang Panlalawigan and of the Office of the Vice-Governor: i. Those provided for in the plantilla of the local government unit concerned and filled up via appointment ii. Those not provided for in the plantilla and hired through job order contracts regardless of the source of funds. As to the employees under letter (a), the Governor has the authority to appoint them. This is already settled in the Villarosa case. With regard to the employees under letter (b) and letter(c)(i), the Vice Governor has the authority to appoint the same. This was also discussed in the Villarosa case. Please be informed that this rule equally applies as well to Mayor and Vice Mayor. However, as to employees under letter (c)(ii) whose items are not so provided in the plantilla of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan and the Office of the Vice-Governor and thus hired only through execution of job order contracts, we find the view that it is the Governor who has the authority to hire them because of the following provisions: Section 77, LGC Section 77. Responsibility for Human Resources and Development. - The chief executive of every local government unit shall be responsible for human resources and development in his unit and shall take all personnel actions in accordance with the Constitutional provisions on civil service, pertinent laws, and rules and regulations thereon, including such policies, guidelines and standards as the Civil Service Commission may establish: Provided, That the local chief executive may employ emergency or casual employees or laborers paid on a daily wage or piecework basis and hired through job orders for local projects authorized by the sanggunian concerned, without need of approval or attestation by the Civil Service Commission: Provided, further, That the period of employment of emergency or casual laborers as provided in this Section shall not exceed six (6) months. The Joint Commission on Local Government Personnel Administration organized pursuant to Presidential Decree Numbered Eleven Hundred thirty-six (P.D. No. 1136) is hereby abolished and its personnel, records, equipment and other assets transferred to the appropriate office in the Civil Service Commission. ji. Represent the province in all its business transactions and sign in its behalf all bonds, contracts, and obligations, and such other documents upon authority of the sangguniang panlalawigan or pursuant to law or ordinance; Page 3 of 7

By declaring that "the authority of the Vice-Governor to appoint the officials and employees of the Sanggunian is anchored on the fact that the salaries of these employees are derived from the appropriation specifically for the said local legislative body, the Supreme Court could not have intended to include those employees enumerated under letter (c)(ii) under the appointing authority of the Vice Governor since job orders result to the execution of contract of services and/or job order contracts. Such intention is shown by the use of the Supreme Court of the terms "appointment" and "appointing power" when referring to casual and job order employees of the Sanggunian. The terms "appointment" and "appointing power" are not used when referring to contract of services and/or job order contracts. The Department, in Legal Opinion No. 89, series of 2022 has opined that since COS/JOs results to the execution of contracts, it necessarily follows that it is the Mayor that has the authority to hire them pursuant to Section 444(b)(i)(vi) of the Local Government Code of 1991 (LGC), viz: Upon authorization by the sangguniang bayan, represent the municipality in all its business transactions and sign on its behalf all bonds, contracts, and obligations, and such other documents made pursuant to law or ordinance. Legal Opinion No. 89, series of 2022 is anchored on Legal Opinion No. 34, series of 2014. The penultimate paragraph of which states: As a general rule, all contracts of services and job orders shall be entered into by the local chief executive of the local government unit, except in cases where there is an ordinance passed by the sanggunian specifically authorizing the vice-mayor or vice-governor to enter into contracts on behalf of the local government unit. We anchored this opinion from the case of Vicencio vs. Villar, et ap, viz: In fact, this absence of inherent authority on the part of the vice-governor to enter into contracts on behalf of the local government unit was reiterated by the Supreme Court in the recent case, Vicencio vs. Villar, et.al., thus: "Section 456. Powers, Duties and Compensation. (a) The city vice-mayor shall: (I) Be the presiding officer of the sangguniang panlungsod and sign all warrants drawn on the city treasury for all expenditures appropriated for the operation of the sangguniang panlungsod; (2) Subject to civil service law, rules and regulations, appoint all officials and employees of the sangguniang panlungsod, except those whose manner of appointment is specifically provided in this Code; 2 G.R. No. 182969, July 3, 2012 Page 4 of 7

(3) Assume the office of the city mayor for the unexpired term of the latter in the event of permanent vacancy as provided for in Section 44, Book I of this Code; (4) Exercise the powers and perform the duties and functions of the city mayor in cases of temporary vacancy as provided for in Section 46, Book I of this Code; and (5) Exercise such other powers and perform such other duties and functions as may be prescribed by law or ordinance. Under this provision, therefore, there is no inherent authority on the part of the city vice-mayor to enter into contracts on behalf of the local government unit, unlike that provided for the city mayor." The Supreme Court nevertheless gave an instance in the same case where the vice-mayor may enter into a contract on behalf of the city, viz "Thus, the authority of the vice-mayor to enter into contracts on behalf of the city was strictly circumscribed by the ordinance granting it. Ordinance No. 15-2003 specially authorized Vice-Mayor Yambao to enter into contracts for consultancy services. As this is not a power or duty given under the law to the Office Of the Vice Mayor, Ordinance No. 15-2003 cannot be construed as •continuing authority' for any person who enters the Office of the Vice- mayor to enter into subsequent, albeit similar contracts." Having presented the pertinent provision of the LGC, and ruling of the SC, we therefore opine that, regardless of the source of fund, it is only the local chief executive that has the authority to hire JOs/COS, unless there is an ordinance specifically authorizing the vice mayor or vice governor to hire them. Meanwhile, we are of the view that contracts that has been executed between the vice mayor/vice governor and the COS/JOs can be ratified, and the same is governed by the following provisions of the Civil Code of the Philippines, viz: ARTICLE 1403. The following contracts are unenforceable, unless they are ratified: (1) Those entered into in the name of another person by one who has been given no authority or legal representation, or who has acted beyond his powers; (2) Those that do not comply with the Statute of Frauds as set forth in this number. In the following cases an agreement hereafter made shall be unenforceable by action, unless the same, or some note or memorandum, thereof, be in writing, and subscribed by the party charged, or by his agent; evidence, therefore, of the agreement cannot be received without the writing, or a secondary evidence of its contents: page 5 of 7

(a) An agreement that by its terms is not to be performed within a year from the making thereof; (b) A special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another; (c) An agreement made in consideration of marriage, other than a mutual promise to marry; (d) An agreement for the sale of goods, chattels or things in action, at a price not less than five hundred pesos, unless the buyer accept and receive part of such goods and chattels, or the evidences, or some of them, of such things in action, or pay at the time some part of the purchase money; but when a sale is made by auction and entry is made by the auctioneer in his sales book, at the time of the sale, of the amount and kind of property sold, terms Of sale, price, names of the purchasers and person on whose account the sale is made, it is a sufficient memorandum; (e) An agreement for the leasing for a longer period than one year, or for the sale of real property or of an interest therein; (f) A representation as to the credit of a third person. (3) Those where both parties are incapable of giving consent to a contract. ARTICLE 1404. Unauthorized contracts are governed by article 1317 and the principles of agency in Title X of this Book. Article 1317 of the Civil Code states: ARTICLE 1317. No one may contract in the name of another without being authorized by the latter, or unless he has by law a right to represent him. A contract entered into in the name of another by one who has no authority or legal representation, or who has acted beyond his powers, shall be unenforceable, unless it is ratified, expressly or impliedly, by the person on whose behalf it has been executed, before it is revoked by the other contracting party. Accordingly, there is a remedy — that is to enact an ordinance, relative to the hiring of JOS, for the contract to be ratified. Ratification may be effected expressly or tacitly. It is understood that there is a tacit ratification if, with knowledge of the reason which renders the contract voidable and such reason having ceased, the person who has a right to invoke it should execute an act which necessarily implies an intention to waive his right3. Ratification cleanses the contract from all its defect from the moment it was constituted4. 3 Article 1393, New Civil Code of the Philippines 4 Article 1396, NCCP Page 6 of 7

Be that as it may, to finally settle the matter, we deem it prudent to request for your further clarification on the matter. Thank you. Respectfully yours, BY AUTH TY OF THE SEC TARY: VI OR R.
